planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall or early spring into acidic, well-drained forest soil; deer oak tolerates heavy winter rain but wants good drainage and a partially shaded site like its native mixed-conifer understory.

directions: Plant in partial shade on acidic, well-drained soil, siting it as an understory thicket shrub rather than a lawn specimen. Deer oak is a shrubby evergreen oak endemic to the Klamath Mountains of southwest Oregon and northwest California, forming dense 6-10 foot thickets under mixed-conifer canopy with broad, glossy, serrated leaves that give it a holly-like texture. It tolerates summer drought once established thanks to its native dry-summer, wet-winter climate, and spreads slowly by root sprouts to form a long-lived colony. Use it as a wildlife thicket or woodland-garden understory shrub in cool, humid-winter climates; it does not perform well in hot, dry, or alkaline conditions.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall into sharply drained, rocky soil in full sun; huckleberry oak is built for thin mountain soils and resents heavy, wet, or fertile ground.

directions: Plant in full sun on sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil, including serpentine; huckleberry oak is a dwarf, mat-forming evergreen shrub oak of exposed ridges from 3,000 to 9,000 feet across the Klamath Ranges and into the southern Cascades and Sierra Nevada. Its small, leathery leaves resemble a huckleberry's, and the low, spreading habit makes it a good choice for rock gardens, dry slopes, or wall plantings where a true tree oak would be too large. Once established it needs essentially no summer water and resents rich or poorly drained soil. Growth is slow, so expect a long-lived, low-maintenance specimen rather than a fast-filling shrub.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall or early spring into acidic, well-drained soil; young trees are shade-tolerant understory saplings and can be sited under existing canopy to establish before growing into full sun.

directions: Plant in partial shade as a young tree on acidic, well-drained soil; tanoak is the dominant evergreen hardwood of Klamath-Siskiyou mixed-evergreen forest, reaching 60-90 feet with fuzzy new growth and acorns that resemble those of true oaks even though it belongs to its own genus, Lithocarpus (sometimes reclassified as Notholithocarpus densiflorus). Saplings tolerate significant shade as forest understory trees before growing up into the canopy, making this a good large-scale shade or woodland tree for cool, humid-winter climates. Note that sudden oak death (caused by Phytophthora ramorum) has caused major tanoak losses in parts of its native range, so gardeners in affected regions should weigh that risk before planting.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall into well-drained soil in part sun to part shade; boxleaf silktassel is more shade-tolerant and compact than its coastal relative Garrya elliptica.

directions: Plant in part sun to part shade on well-drained soil; boxleaf silktassel is an upright evergreen shrub to about 6 feet, a Klamath-Siskiyou near-endemic with small, leathery, box-like leaves and the pendant catkin flowers typical of the genus Garrya, opening in late winter. It is more compact and shade-tolerant than the widely grown coastal silktassel (Garrya elliptica), making it a useful woodland-garden substitute where a smaller, understory-scale evergreen shrub is wanted. Once established it needs little summer irrigation and tolerates the lean, rocky soils typical of its native mixed-evergreen forest habitat.

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants into sharply drained rock crevices or scree in spring; this fern is built for mineral soil and serpentine rock, not an ordinary shaded fern bed.

directions: Plant in full sun in sharply drained rock crevices or mineral scree; Indian's dream fern is a small, cedar-scented lace fern that forms dense tufts in serpentine and other ultramafic rock outcrops across the Klamath region and intermountain West. Unlike most ferns it is a sun-loving, drought-tolerant rock-garden specialist, needing essentially no irrigation once established in a lean, fast-draining site. It is a genuine specialty-nursery plant rather than a big-box offering, so source it from an alpine or native-plant specialist and expect slow establishment in the first year or two.

planting.note: Set container plants or offsets into gritty, fast-draining soil in spring; roseflower stonecrop grows on rocky slopes and serpentine outcrops and resents heavy or constantly wet ground.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade on gritty, fast-draining soil, including rocky or serpentine sites; roseflower stonecrop is a blue-green rosette succulent native to rocky slopes and serpentine outcrops of the Klamath-Siskiyou region and North Coast Ranges. It blooms pink to pale yellow in early summer on short flowering stems rising from the tight basal rosettes, and makes a good rock-garden or succulent-bed plant in climates with dry summers. Avoid rich soil or regular summer irrigation, which encourages rot rather than the compact growth this species shows in its native lean-soil habitat.

planting.note: Set container plants into shaded, consistently moist, rocky or mossy soil in fall; this is a short-lived perennial best treated as a self-sowing seep-side filler rather than a permanent anchor plant.

directions: Plant in shade to part shade in consistently moist, rocky or mossy soil, mimicking the shaded seeps, wet rock faces, and streambanks it grows on in the wild. California mistmaiden is a low rosette perennial bearing small white, saxifrage-like flowers in late winter and early spring, and it dies back after flowering, often persisting through self-sown seedlings rather than a long-lived single crown. It is a good small-scale filler for a shaded moisture niche such as a seep, bog edge, or damp rock garden where little else of this scale will grow. Supply from specialty native-plant nurseries is thin and seasonal, so expect to buy small plants or seed rather than mature stock.

planting.note: Set divisions into constantly wet, mineral-poor, serpentine-influenced bog substrate in spring; grow it exactly as you would a companion Darlingtonia californica, in the same boggy seep conditions.

directions: Grow in constant boggy moisture on mineral-poor, serpentine-influenced substrate in part shade, the same seepage conditions favored by its frequent habitat companion Darlingtonia californica. Horned butterwort is a rosette-forming carnivorous perennial that catches small insects on sticky, glandular leaves, sending up violet, horn-spurred flowers in spring above the foliage. Use a lean, peat-and-sand or native serpentine-gravel mix kept constantly saturated with mineral-poor (rain or distilled) water, never fertilized garden soil. It is a true carnivorous-plant-specialist item, best sourced from a dedicated carnivorous plant nursery rather than a general garden center.
